analysis.one_liner: Protects millions of acres of Northern Rockies public land as wilderness, wildlife corridors, and wild rivers, ending most logging, mining, and drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 72 House supporters, including three Republicans, but the House Resources Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have designated about 13 million acres of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Oregon, and Washington as wilderness, connecting them with millions more acres of protected wildlife corridors, new wild and scenic rivers, and two new national park studies. Wilderness designation is the strongest land protection in U.S. law: no logging roads, no timber sales, no mining claims, no oil and gas drilling. It would also have created a federal Wildland Recovery Corps to restore damaged forest land and guaranteed Native American access to sacred sites in the protected areas.
analysis.who_benefits: Hikers, hunters, anglers, and everyone downstream who drinks water from Rocky Mountain headwaters would gain permanently protected wild land. The bill specifically guarantees Native American tribes, including the Blackfeet, continued access for religious and traditional uses. Taxpayers also benefit under the bill's own reasoning: it cites federal findings that these roadless forests are worth more left standing than the Treasury earns from logging them, meaning taxpayers stop subsidizing money-losing timber sales.

how_it_helps.text: Designates wilderness across six major ecosystems — including the Greater Yellowstone, Greater Glacier, and Greater Salmon/Selway regions — totaling about 13.4 million acres, plus roughly 4.85 million more acres of connecting corridors.
Prohibits road building, logging, mining, and oil and gas development inside wilderness areas and special corridor management areas, protecting habitat for grizzly bears, wolves, caribou, and salmon.
Creates a National Wildland Restoration and Recovery System and a Wildland Recovery Corps to repair lands damaged by clearcutting and road building, such as clearcuts along the Yellowstone boundary.

Guarantees Native American tribes nonexclusive access to protected areas for traditional cultural and religious purposes, and designates the Badger-Two Medicine area as the Blackfeet Wilderness with recognized treaty rights.
Reserves enough water in each wilderness area to fulfill its purpose, protecting stream flows from future diversion claims.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies, hardrock miners, and oil and gas firms would lose access to millions of acres of federal land they can currently lease or log, and communities built around those jobs would bear the economic adjustment. Taxpayers would fund the new restoration corps and land acquisition programs. Off-road vehicle users and some motorized hunters would lose access to designated wilderness, though the bill explicitly exempts all major highways and state roads and compels no private landowner.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas firms

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation bans motorized travel, so snowmobilers, off-road vehicle riders, and hunters who rely on motorized access would be excluded from about 13 million acres, and the bill bans new road construction across roughly 2.5 million more acres of corridor land.

Timber-dependent towns in Idaho, Montana, and surrounding states would lose access to federal timber supply, and the bill acknowledges the Treasury gives up logging revenue in exchange for the conservation value.
The bill authorizes appropriations for a new Wildland Recovery Corps, park studies, and monitoring programs — a new ongoing federal expense at a time of budget tightening.
Pending national park studies, areas like Hells Canyon would be frozen against new roads, logging, and mining even before Congress decided whether to create the parks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conservation gains are large and permanent: an intact wild ecosystem the size of a small state, cleaner water, and habitat for endangered species, paid for mainly by industries that profit from developing public land. The real costs fall on a small number of timber- and mining-dependent rural communities, which is the strongest good-faith objection — wilderness protection is permanent, and displaced workers get nothing in this bill to ease the transition. Off-road recreation users also lose access. On balance the bill trades narrow, subsidized extractive use for a broad, durable public good, though its one-size-fits-all approach to millions of acres gave local opponents real grounds to object.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Resources Committee and then to two subcommittees, where it sat for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Shays, a Republican from Connecticut, introduced the bill on April 23, 1997, with 24 original cosponsors from both parties.
It was referred to the House Committee on Resources, which in turn referred it to the Subcommittee on National Parks and Public Lands and the Subcommittee on Forests and Forest Health.
The committee asked for executive comments from the Departments of Agriculture and the Interior, but no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the rest of the Congress.
The bill accumulated 71 cosponsors — 67 Democrats, one Independent, and three Republicans — but never reached the House floor.
It died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, leaving the roadless areas it named open to the same logging, mining, and road-building the bill was written to stop.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies kept unrestricted access to the roadless national forest lands the bill would have protected, and the House Resources Committee leadership avoided a vote on a bill with 72 sponsors.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 67 of 71 cosponsors — but the sponsor was a Republican and three Republicans cosponsored, so the bill had a bipartisan core even though committee inaction kept it from a vote where the partisan split would have shown.

industries.note: The bill bans timber harvest and road building across millions of acres of national forest, ending logging in the remaining roadless wildlands of the Northern Rockies. The bill's own findings say these sales cost taxpayers more than they return, so the industry loses a subsidized supply at the public's expense.
New wilderness areas are withdrawn from the mining laws, ending new claims on roughly 13 million acres. Mining on public land imposes reclamation and water quality costs that fall on the public.

The bill prohibits oil and gas leasing and drilling in wilderness areas, corridors, and study areas, and withdraws the Blackfeet Wilderness from mineral leasing. Public lands would no longer be open for extraction.

industries.industry: Motorized recreation and off-road vehicle interests
industries.note: Wilderness designation excludes snowmobiles and off-road vehicles, shrinking the terrain available for motorized use — though the bill explicitly keeps all major highways and state roads open.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation, tourism, and restoration trades
industries.note: The bill creates a Wildland Recovery Corps and preserves scenic wild lands that anchor the region's recreation economy, generating restoration and guide-service work that depends on intact land.
